stories.title_en: Luring Him to Drink and Whore, Ruining His Name

paragraphs.zh: 石涓，湖广麻城人。富而多诈，负气好胜，与族兄石涧尝争买田宅致隙。涧男石孝，读书进学，人品俊秀，性敏能文，人多拟其可中。石涓尝怀妒忌，思“吾生平发财，被涧兄所压。今其子又居士列，是虎而辅翼也。”因思计暗伤涧、孝父子。
paragraphs.en: Shi Juan was a man of Macheng in Huguang. He was rich but full of tricks, proud and competitive. He and his clan elder brother Shi Jian had often quarreled over buying fields and houses, and a grudge grew between them. Jian’s son Shi Xiao studied, entered the county school, was handsome in person, quick-witted, and good at writing; people often guessed he might pass the provincial examination. Shi Juan nursed jealousy: “All my life I have made money, yet I have been overshadowed by elder brother Jian. Now his son has joined the ranks of licentiates—a tiger given wings.” So he thought of a plan to harm Jian and Xiao, father and son, in secret.

paragraphs.zh: 不数年，涧故。石孝居忧，无人检束。涓思孝年少不羁，或可诱以酒色。因伪相结纳，孝趋亦趋，孝诺亦诺，终日游戏相征逐，数以曲蘖为欢。或时有美妓，涓邀孝饮其邸；或有好戏妇，涓每搬戏邀孝饮，又令戏妇曲意奉承，务挑其淫荡之心。孝堕其术中而不觉，玩日月，荒废诗书。及服阕补考，竟列劣等。孝因发奋，往寺读书，涓辄拉友挟妓，载酒至寺欢饮。孝见妓，不觉有喜心，故态复萌。涓又劝孝娶美妾二人，朝夕纵淫。内荒于色，外湎于酒，手沾战疯，不能楷书。道考被黜，家业凋零。石涓抚掌大笑曰：“吾生平之恨泄矣，计亦遂矣！”乃呼其子而训之曰：“涧兄在日，家富于我。因生孝不肖，酷好饮酒宿娼，不事诗书，致令丧却前程，身如丧家之狗。尔辈宜以为鉴，慎勿踏其覆辙。”未几，其子亦被人引诱赌嫖，所费不訾。涓因年老，无如之何，唯付之长叹而已。
paragraphs.en: Within a few years Jian died. Shi Xiao was in mourning, with no one to keep him in check. Juan thought: Xiao is young and unrestrained; perhaps he can be lured with wine and women. So he pretended to draw close. Wherever Xiao went, Juan went; whatever Xiao agreed to, Juan agreed to. They spent whole days chasing amusement, and often made merry with wine. When there was a pretty courtesan, Juan would invite Xiao to drink at her lodgings; when there was a fetching actress, Juan would put on a play, invite Xiao to drink, and have the actress fawn on him in every way, determined to stir his lust. Xiao fell into the trap without noticing. He played away the days and months and neglected his books. When mourning ended and he sat the makeup examination, he was ranked in the lowest class. Xiao then resolved to study at a temple. Juan would drag friends and courtesans along, bringing wine to the temple to drink. Seeing the courtesans, Xiao could not help feeling pleased, and his old ways returned. Juan then urged Xiao to take two beautiful concubines, and they indulged in lust morning and night. Inside he was wasted by sex; outside he was soaked in wine. A shaking palsy got into his hands, and he could not write regular script. At the circuit examination he was struck off the rolls, and the family estate withered. Shi Juan clapped his hands and laughed: “The hatred of my whole life is vented; my plan has succeeded!” He then called his sons and instructed them: “While elder brother Jian lived, his household was richer than mine. Because he sired the worthless Xiao, who loved drinking and visiting prostitutes and would not tend to his books, he lost his prospects and became like a stray dog. You should take this as a warning, and be careful not to follow in his tracks.” Before long, his own sons were also lured by others into gambling and whoring, and the expenses were enormous. Juan was old and could do nothing about it; he could only heave long sighs.

paragraphs.zh: 按：石涓奸巧百端，匿怨友人，使孝淫溺酒色，名利俱丧。彼虽自谓得计，足以快其宿忿，殊不思杀人之父，人亦杀其父；杀人之兄，人亦杀其兄。天网恢恢，报应不爽，安能保他人不袭彼故智，而子孙不蹈其覆辙乎？垂戒二子所繇，殆与义方之训异矣，又何怪其子之复然耶！然孝亦自愚也。使孝稍有心智，宜忖父在之时，与彼有怨，今父已即世，得彼不念足矣，顾安望深交乃尔！此其中情，叵测可知。由是以怠惰荒淫为戒，勤励不息自强，则石涓虽诈，安能中自立之士哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: Shi Juan was cunning in a hundred ways. He hid his resentment while befriending, and made Xiao drown in wine and lust until name and profit were both lost. He thought he had succeeded and could vent his old anger, but he did not consider: if you kill a man’s father, someone will kill yours; if you kill a man’s elder brother, someone will kill yours. Heaven’s net is wide; retribution does not miss. How could he be sure others would not copy his old trick, and that his own sons and grandsons would not follow the same path? The warning he gave his two sons was quite unlike a proper father’s instruction—no wonder his sons turned out the same! Yet Xiao was foolish too. If Xiao had had even a little sense, he should have thought: while Father lived, this man was his enemy; now Father is dead, it is enough if the man does not nurse the grudge—how could one hope for such deep friendship! From this, the man’s hidden feelings were clearly unfathomable. Had Xiao taken sloth and lust as a warning and worked hard without pause, then even if Shi Juan were crafty, how could he have struck a man who stood on his own feet?

stories.title_en: Luring a Friend into Adultery to Scheme for His Land

paragraphs.zh: 毕和，山西人。心术狡险，阴悍暗毒，乡人无不被其害者。族弟毕松，有田一段，价值五十餘金，与和田毗连。和屡谋不遂，因诈与交好，屡席相款，旦夕游戏，即同胞不啻焉。
paragraphs.en: Bi He was a man of Shanxi. His mind was sly and vicious, secretly fierce and poisonous; there was hardly a villager he had not harmed. His clan younger brother Bi Song had a plot of land worth more than fifty taels, adjoining He’s fields. He had often schemed for it without success, so he pretended friendship, repeatedly treated Song to feasts, and amused himself with him morning and evening, no less close than full brothers.

paragraphs.zh: 同乡有林远者，性刚而暴。其妻罗氏，貌美好淫，与夫反睦〔目〕。和乘机挑之，遂通往来，情甚密。假意不令松知，实欲使之知之。故遮头露尾，为松觑破。松乃怪和曰：“枉自与你相知。有此美妇人，何不引我一宿，岂便夺你爱乎？”和逊谢曰：“此妇极有情，若引你去，必深相怜爱。恐你往来无节，事机不密，其夫若知，有误身家不便矣。”松只疑其专宠，乃私往挑之，罗氏遂允。后来情更绸缪，每候其夫出外，非和往则松往，甚且三人同床，情如一体。
paragraphs.en: In the same village was Lin Yuan, harsh and violent by nature. His wife, née Luo, was beautiful and lustful, and she and her husband were at odds. He took the chance to seduce her; they began to meet, and grew very close. He pretended not to let Song know, but in fact wanted Song to find out. So he covered the head and left the tail showing, until Song caught on. Song then blamed He: “It’s wasted that I call you a friend. With such a beautiful woman, why not bring me for one night? Would I snatch away your favorite?” He declined modestly: “This woman is very affectionate. If I bring you, she will surely dote on you. I fear you would come and go without restraint, the affair would not stay secret, and if her husband found out, it would endanger your person and household.” Song only suspected He of hogging her, so he went privately to seduce her, and Luo agreed. Later their passion grew even thicker. Whenever the husband went out, if it was not He who went, it was Song; sometimes even the three of them shared a bed, as close as one body.

paragraphs.zh: 将及月餘，和密报其夫曰：“松弟与我至知，今闻与令正有情，我屡谏不听。闻你欲捕之，若捕得，可轻打些。彼必叫我解交，我谕他多送你些银，以绝他后日妄为。慎勿害他性命。”林远闻言，怒气填胸。次日即托言外出，须三日后方归。松专瞰远去向，闻其出外，即往其家，搂罗氏入房调耍。林远从密处突出，打入房中，二人已解衣在床。远揪松于床下凶打，罗氏拼命拿住夫手，远不能多打。松求放曰：“愿以银赎免。”远曰：“要何人来保认？”松曰：“叫我和兄来。”远正合意，即遣人呼和至。和曰：“不行正路，以至于此。须召见你亲兄来。”松曰：“勿召我兄，只你代我出银与之，后日即还。”和曰：“我代议事，怎好出银？但今事急矣，我若不出银，此事无由解释。然必有实物相当方可。”松因写前毗连之田契卖之。和曰：“只可少作价，多则亦为林远所得。”止作价四十两。和归，取银三十两相付。远曰：“须六十两。”和曰：“奸情被获，合输妇价一半。纵令正美貌，可值六十金，此已一半矣。”远再三不肯。和曰：“彼田价四十两，我手中无现银，不如约一月后，再在我手接十两。”远要约批。和曰：“若他人议事，须加二抽头，我已该八两矣。今为你息事，何逼我约批乎？”遂无约批，放松同归。
paragraphs.en: After about a month, He secretly told the husband: “Younger brother Song and I are closest friends, but I hear he has an affair with your wife. I have advised him many times and he will not listen. I hear you mean to catch them. If you catch them, beat him only lightly. He will surely call me to mediate. I will tell him to give you a good deal of silver, to stop his later recklessness. Be careful not to take his life.” Lin Yuan heard this, and rage filled his chest. The next day he pretended to go out, saying he would return only after three days. Song watched closely which way Yuan went; hearing he had gone out, he went to the house, embraced Luo, and took her into the room to sport. Lin Yuan burst from a hiding place into the room; the two had already undressed on the bed. Yuan dragged Song off the bed and beat him fiercely. Luo clung to her husband’s arms with all her strength, so Yuan could not beat him much. Song begged to be let go: “I am willing to redeem myself with silver.” Yuan said: “Who will stand surety?” Song said: “Call my elder cousin He.” This suited Yuan exactly; he sent someone to fetch He. He said: “You did not walk the proper road, and it has come to this. You must summon your own elder brother.” Song said: “Do not summon my brother. Just put up the silver for me; I will repay you later.” He said: “I am mediating—how can I put up the silver? But the matter is urgent. If I do not put it up, there is no way to settle this. There must be something of matching value.” Song then wrote a deed selling the adjoining field. He said: “You can only put it at a low price; if it is high, Lin Yuan will get that much more.” They put it at only forty taels. He went home, fetched thirty taels, and handed them over. Yuan said: “I want sixty taels.” He said: “Caught in adultery, you ought to pay half a wife’s price. Even if your wife is beautiful and worth sixty taels, this is already half.” Yuan refused again and again. He said: “His field is priced at forty taels. I have no ready silver on me. Better to agree that a month later he will receive another ten taels from my hand.” Yuan wanted a written note. He said: “If anyone else mediated, he would take a twenty percent cut—I would already be due eight taels. Now I am settling this for you; why force me to write a note?” So there was no note, and he let Song go home with him.

paragraphs.zh: 数日后，松备本息四十四两赎前田，和不肯退。一月后，林远向和取约银。和曰：“指示你撰银三十两，二两谢我，岂为多乎？”远后对人说出和教捉奸之由，松方知为和所卖。然已堕其诡计，悔无及矣。
paragraphs.en: A few days later Song prepared principal and interest, forty-four taels, to redeem the field; He would not return it. A month later Lin Yuan went to He for the promised silver. He said: “I showed you how to get thirty taels. Two taels as thanks to me—is that too much?” Yuan later told others that He had taught him to catch the adultery; only then did Song know he had been sold by He. But he had already fallen into the trap, and regret was too late.

paragraphs.zh: 按：和欲谋松田，先引之奸；欲诱其奸，先与之友。且其奸也，非彼明引，而令其自入。其要之田也，俟其有急而为之解纷，以徐收之，计亦巧矣。向非赖后约银，则林远必不言其所由，彼和之深情厚毒，畴能测之？故人而毒行不端者，彼虽与我交密，亦须提防者也。
paragraphs.en: Note: He wanted Song’s land, so first he led him into adultery; to lure him into adultery, he first made friends with him. And the adultery was not something He openly led him into—he made Song walk in himself. As for demanding the land, he waited until Song was in a pinch, then “settled the quarrel” for him, and slowly took it. The scheme was clever. If not for the later promised silver, Lin Yuan would never have told how it started, and who could have fathomed He’s deep friendship and thick poison? So if a man is vicious and does not walk a proper path, even if he is close with you, you must still be on guard.

stories.title_en: Piling Up a Friend’s Debts Until His House Collapses

paragraphs.zh: 金从宇、洪起予，俱是应天府人。相隔一十餘店，皆开大京铺，各有资本千餘金。但从宇狡猾奸险，起予温良朴实。时常贩买京货，累相会席，各有酒量，欢相劝酬。
paragraphs.en: Jin Congyu and Hong Qiyu were both of Yingtian Prefecture. They were a little more than ten shops apart, both keeping large capital shops, each with over a thousand taels of capital. But Congyu was sly and vicious, while Qiyu was mild, kind, and simple. They often bought capital goods, repeatedly met at banquets, both had a capacity for wine, and cheerfully pledged cups.

paragraphs.zh: 从宇思曰：“人言慈不掌兵，义不掌财。我观起予慈善好义，诚直无智。何彼铺买卖与我相并也？当以智术笼络之。”以故伪相交密，时节以物相馈送，有庆贺礼，皆相请召。起予只以金为好意，皆薄来厚往以答之。从宇曰：“此人好酒，须以酒误之。”乃时时饮月福、打平和、邀庆纲，招饮殆无虚日。有芳辰佳景，邀与同游；夜月清凉，私谈竟夕。起予果中其奸，日在醉乡，不事买卖。从宇虽日伴起予游饮，彼有弟济宇在店，凡事皆能代理。起予一向闲游，店中虚无人守。有客来店者，寻之不在，多往济宇铺买。由是金铺日盛，洪铺日替，起予渐穷于用。从宇随取随与之，每一半九成，一半七八成；银又等头轻少，不索其借批，但云“须明白记帐也”。不四五年间，陆续借上六百餘两。乃使济宇往取之，起予别借二百两以还。后算过帐，尚欠四百餘两。逼其写田宅为当，方思还债取田。起予一皆从言。再过两年，本息合四百五十餘两矣。济宇力逼全收。起予求从宇稍宽。从宇曰：“吾银本与舍弟相共，彼在家尝怨我不合把银借你。今我不理，任你两下何如？”此时金宅有新立当契在手，起予推延不过，只得将产业尽数写契填还之。他债主知其落寞，都来逼取。千餘金家，不两三栽，一旦罄空。皆金从宇倾陷累算之故也。
paragraphs.en: Congyu thought: “People say the merciful do not command troops, and the righteous do not command wealth. I see Qiyu is kind and fond of doing right, honest and without cunning. How is it his shop’s trade equals mine? I should use clever arts to snare him.” So he pretended close friendship, sent gifts at festivals, and invited him to every celebration. Qiyu took Jin’s acts as goodwill, and always answered thin gifts with thick ones. Congyu said: “This man loves wine; I must ruin him with wine.” So he constantly held monthly-blessing drinks, share-the-cost feasts, and guild celebrations, inviting him to drink almost without a free day. On fair days and fine views he invited him to roam together; on cool moonlit nights they talked privately until dawn. Qiyu indeed fell for the trick, living day after day in drunkenness and neglecting his business. Though Congyu spent his days drinking and roaming with Qiyu, he had a younger brother, Jiyu, in the shop who could manage everything. Qiyu idled about, and no one watched his shop. Customers who came and found him gone mostly went to buy at Jiyu’s shop. Thus Jin’s shop grew daily, Hong’s declined daily, and Qiyu gradually ran short of money. Congyu would give whenever asked: half of it ninety-percent silver, half of it seventy- or eighty-percent silver; the scale-weight was also light. He did not demand a loan note, only saying, “Just keep a clear account.” In less than four or five years, the loans added up to more than six hundred taels. He then sent Jiyu to collect. Qiyu borrowed two hundred taels elsewhere to repay. After the accounts were reckoned, he still owed more than four hundred. They pressed him to mortgage fields and houses, thinking later to repay the debt and redeem the land. Qiyu agreed to everything they said. Two more years passed; principal and interest together came to more than four hundred fifty taels. Jiyu pressed hard to collect in full. Qiyu begged Congyu to ease up a little. Congyu said: “My silver capital is shared with my younger brother. At home he often blames me for wrongly lending you silver. Now I will not intervene; do as you two will.” By then the Jin household held a newly written mortgage deed. Qiyu could not put it off, and had to write deeds for all his property to fill the debt. Other creditors, seeing him ruined, all came to press for payment. A household of over a thousand taels, within two or three years, was emptied at a stroke. All this was Jin Congyu’s trapping and compounding.

paragraphs.zh: 洪已破家之后，从宇全不瞅睐，虽求分文相借，一毫不与矣。从宇又用此术，再交杨店之子。有识者笑杨子曰：“汝是洪起予替身，何不取鉴前车乎？”杨乃渐疏绝之。
paragraphs.en: After Hong’s household was broken, Congyu paid him no attention at all; even if he asked to borrow a single cash, he would not give a hair. Congyu then used the same trick to befriend the son of the Yang shop. Those who understood laughed at young Yang: “You are Hong Qiyu’s stand-in. Why not take warning from the cart ahead?” Yang then gradually kept him at a distance.

paragraphs.zh: 按：以银借人，收其子利，未为累算。特洪本富贾，从宇诱其游饮，不事生理，致资本消折，而以银借之。期间以八当十，加三算息，亏短田价，稍蚕食之。从宇之奸贪极矣！为富不仁，从宇其何说之辞？
paragraphs.en: Note: Lending silver to others and taking interest is not, by itself, compounding a trap. The point is that Hong was originally a rich merchant, and Congyu lured him into roaming and drinking so he neglected his livelihood, his capital shrank, and then he lent him silver. In between he counted eight as ten, charged thirty percent interest, shorted the land price, and slowly ate him like a silkworm. Congyu’s greed and treachery reached the extreme! The rich who are not humane—what excuse can Congyu offer?

stories.title_en: Goading a Friend into an Adultery Suit to Ruin His House

paragraphs.zh: 马自鸣，浙江绍兴人。狷巧小人，柔媚多奸。族弟马应，轻浮愚昧，家更富于自鸣。其父素与鸣父不睦，两相图而未发。自鸣见应愚呆，性又嗜酒，故时时与之会饮；亦连引诸人，共打平和。唯此两人深相结纳，人多厌之，不与共饮。二人乃对斟对酌，此唱彼和，自号为莫逆交。应有事，多取决于自鸣；鸣亦时献小计，以效忠款。应素与亲兄不睦，数扬其短，欲状告之。自鸣假意劝阻，实于当机处反言以激之，益深其怒。应遂先往告兄，经官断明，拟应欧兄之罪；又投分上解释。此为破家之始。又屡屡唆其与人争讼，家日破败。
paragraphs.en: Ma Ziming was a man of Shaoxing in Zhejiang. A petty, clever man, soft-spoken and full of tricks. His clan younger brother Ma Ying was flighty and foolish, and his household was even richer than Ziming’s. Ying’s father had long been on bad terms with Ming’s father; both sides plotted against each other but had not yet struck. Ziming saw that Ying was stupid and also loved wine, so he often drank with him, and also brought others along to split the cost. Only these two became closely bound; others grew tired of them and would not drink with them. The two then pledged cups face to face, singing in answer, calling themselves sworn friends. When Ying had affairs, he often took Ziming’s advice; Ming would also offer small schemes from time to time, to show loyal feeling. Ying had long been on bad terms with his own elder brother, often aired his faults, and wanted to file a complaint. Ziming pretended to dissuade him, but at the crucial points used reverse words to goad him, deepening his anger. Ying then went first to accuse his brother. The officials judged clearly and sentenced Ying for beating an elder brother; they also used connections to settle it. This was the start of the family’s ruin. He then repeatedly incited Ying to sue others, and the household grew more broken by the day.

paragraphs.zh: 后自鸣往小户人家取债，见其妇幼美，归家向应前夸曰：“我今往某家取债，其媳妇生甚美貌，女流中西施也。我以目挑之，俯首而过。其屋只一楹，数往来于前。我神魂飘荡，不能自禁。又以笑语挑之，此妇亦笑脸回答，似亦可图。只怕其夫姑有碍，未敢施为。至今挂恋在心，寤寐思服。”应曰：“此家是我甲首，又系佃户，图亦何难？我必先取之。”自鸣激之曰：“汝若能得，我输你一大东道。依我说，勿去惹此愚夫，若捉住，彼粗拳，真打死也。”应曰：“未闻佃客敢殴主人者。”次日，即往其家收条编。一见其妇，即挑之，遣其婆出外曰：“可外出觅菜来作午。”婆方出，即强抱其妇入房。妇在从否之间，见隔壁一妇窥见躲开。妇指之曰：“某姆在隔壁窥见，你勿为此。”哪肯休，只以为推托也。相缠已久，婆在外归。妇只得叫妈妈曰：“主人如此野意。”婆作色叱。怒，先往县呈其拖欠条编，反允殴里长。其佃人以强奸诉官拘审，邻妇窥见，亲姑捉获。其妇又貌美倾城，满堂聚观，啧啧叹赏。因审作强奸，应拟死罪。后投分上，改作戏奸未就。而家业尽倾，田宅皆卖与自鸣。（自鸣）反责曰：“我当初叫你勿为，你不听吾言，以至于此。”应曰：“你口虽叫我勿为，先已造桥，送我在桥中去矣，难回步也。今欲怪你，又怪不得。孟子谓‘非之无可举，刺之无可刺’，正你这样人也。”
paragraphs.en: Later Ziming went to a small household to collect a debt, saw the young wife was beautiful, and came home and boasted to Ying: “I went to such-and-such a house to collect a debt. The daughter-in-law is extremely beautiful, a Xi Shi among women. I glanced at her; she passed with her head down. The house has only one bay; I went back and forth in front of it several times. My soul was adrift; I could not restrain myself. I teased her with smiles and words; she answered with a smiling face, as if she might be had. I only feared her husband and mother-in-law would be in the way, and did not dare act. To this day I keep thinking of her, even in sleep.” Ying said: “That household is among my jia households, and they are also my tenants. What is hard about getting her? I will take her first.” Ziming goaded him: “If you can get her, I will lose you a big treat. Take my advice: don’t provoke that stupid husband. If he catches you, those coarse fists will truly beat you to death.” Ying said: “I have never heard of a tenant daring to beat his landlord.” The next day he went to that house to collect the combined tax. As soon as he saw the woman, he teased her, and sent her mother-in-law out: “Go out and find some vegetables for lunch.” Once the old woman had gone, he forcibly embraced the wife into the room. The woman was between yielding and refusing; she saw a woman next door peeking and then hiding. She pointed and said: “Auntie So-and-so next door saw; don’t do this.” He would not stop, taking it as an excuse. They had been tangled a long time when the mother-in-law came back from outside. The wife had to call “Mama”: “The master is being this wild.” The old woman scolded angrily. Enraged, Ying first went to the county and charged them with defaulting on the combined tax, and even with beating the village head. The tenant accused him of rape; officials arrested and tried them. The neighboring woman had seen it, and the mother-in-law had caught them. The wife was also beautiful enough to topple a city; the whole hall gathered to look, clucking in admiration. They tried it as rape, and Ying was sentenced to death. Later, using connections, it was changed to sporting toward adultery, not completed. But the family estate was entirely gone; fields and houses were all sold to Ziming. Ziming instead scolded: “At the start I told you not to do it; you would not listen, and it has come to this.” Ying said: “Your mouth told me not to, but you had already built the bridge and sent me onto it, so I could not turn back. Now I want to blame you, yet I cannot quite. Mencius said, ‘You cannot point to what is wrong, cannot pick out what to stab’—that is exactly a man like you.”

paragraphs.zh: 田卖尽，自鸣绝不与往来。朝夕相借，惟干谒亲兄，方知亲者终是亲；彼酒肉朋友，真伪情也。
paragraphs.en: When the land was sold out, Ziming cut off all dealings. Morning and evening Ying had to borrow; only when he went begging to his own elder brother did he know that kin are kin in the end, and those wine-and-meat friends were false feeling.

paragraphs.zh: 按：应被自鸣笼络，家破，产业尽被鸣收之，反与之莫逆之交，何其愚也！苟有心智人之处世，内而兄弟叔侄，外而朋友亲戚，皆不能无。与兄结讼而求昵于友，是其所厚者薄，而薄者反厚也。何不观孙荣之间革孙华而亦昵于友，使非杨氏贤德，后始有悔悟。而能以是而自新之，彼虽有百般巧计，安能中自新之士哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: Ying was snared by Ziming; his house was broken, his property all taken by Ming, and yet he had treated him as a sworn friend—how foolish! If a man of any sense lives in the world, within he has brothers, uncles, and nephews; without he has friends and relatives—none can be done without. To sue one’s brother and seek intimacy with a friend is to treat the near as distant and the distant as near. Why not look at Sun Rong, who discarded Sun Hua and likewise clung to a friend? If not for Lady Yang’s worthy virtue, only later would there have been regret and awakening. If one can take this and renew oneself, then even with a hundred clever schemes, how can they strike a man who has made himself new?

stories.title_en: A Cunning Broker Dumps Paper and Pays with His Daughter

paragraphs.zh: 施守训，福建大安人。家资殷富，常造纸卖客。一日，自装千餘篓，价值八百餘两，往苏州卖，寓牙人翁滨二店。滨乃宿牙，叠积前客债甚多，见施雏商，将其纸尽还前客，误施坐候半年。家中又发纸五百餘篓到苏州，滨代现卖。付银讫，托言系取旧帐者，复候半年。知受其笼络，施乃怒骂殴之。滨无言可应，当凭乡亲刘光前议，谕滨立过借批银八百两，劝施暂回。
paragraphs.en: Shi Shouxun was a man of Da’an in Fujian. His household was wealthy; he often made paper and sold it to merchants. One day he packed more than a thousand baskets, worth over eight hundred taels, went to Suzhou to sell, and lodged at the shop of the broker Weng Bin’er. Bin was a veteran broker, stacked with many debts to earlier clients. Seeing Shi was a greenhorn merchant, he used all the paper to repay previous clients, and kept Shi waiting half a year. The household then sent another five hundred-odd baskets of paper to Suzhou; Bin sold them for ready money. After the silver was paid over, he claimed it was for collecting old accounts, and Shi waited another half year. Knowing he had been snared, Shi then cursed and beat him. Bin had no words to answer. On the mediation of fellow-townsman Liu Guangqian, they instructed Bin to write a loan note for eight hundred taels of silver, and advised Shi to go home for the time being.

paragraphs.zh: 次年，复载纸到苏州，滨代现卖。只前帐难还，施又坐待半年。见其女云英有貌，未曾许配，思此银难取，乃浼刘光前为媒，求其女为妾，抵还前帐。滨悦许之。其女年方十五，执不肯从。滨与妻入劝曰：“古有缇萦愿没官为婢，以赎父罪。今父欠客人银八百两，以汝填还；况福建客家多巨富，若后日生子，分其家财，居此致富，享福非小。”女始允诺。时施已六十餘矣。成婚近四载，施后回家身故。未及周期服，滨将女重嫁南京溧水县梁恩赐为妾，重收聘礼一百两。
paragraphs.en: The next year Shi again loaded paper to Suzhou; Bin sold it for ready money. Only the old account was hard to repay, and Shi waited another half year. He saw Bin’s daughter Yunying was pretty and not yet betrothed. Thinking this silver would be hard to collect, he asked Liu Guangqian to act as matchmaker, seeking the daughter as a concubine to offset the old account. Bin gladly agreed. The girl was just fifteen and firmly would not consent. Bin and his wife went in and advised her: “In ancient times Tiying was willing to become an official slave to redeem her father’s crime. Now Father owes a client eight hundred taels; we fill it with you. Besides, Fujian merchant houses are often very rich. If later you bear a son and share the family wealth, you will live here in riches and enjoy no small fortune.” The girl then agreed. Shi was already over sixty. They were married nearly four years; later Shi went home and died. Before a full year of mourning, Bin remarried the girl as concubine to Liang Enci of Lishui county, Nanjing, and again took a betrothal gift of one hundred taels.

paragraphs.zh: 守训男施钦知之为，本年亦装纸到苏州，往拜翁家，呼翁为“外祖”。翁不瞅睬他。请庶母出见，亦拒不出。众客伙皆怒而嗾曰：“你父以八百两聘礼，止成亲四载，未期服又重嫁他人。今一出见何害？情甚可恶！汝何不鸣官？”钦乃告于巡街蔡御史。时翁滨二得施为婿，复振家风，又发资金千餘，见告，毫无惧意。两下各投分上，讦讼几二年。各司道皆纳分上，附会而判。后钦状告刑部，始获公断曰：“翁滨二以女抵偿八百两，几与绿珠同价矣。但守训自肯，其财礼勿论。今夫服未满重嫁梁客，兜重财物，是以女为货，不顾律法。合责三十板，断身资银一百两，并守训为云英置衣资首饰银五十两，共与施钦领之。”因此积讼连年，滨二之家财尽倾，仍流落于贫矣。
paragraphs.en: Shouxun’s son Shi Qin learned of this. That same year he also packed paper to Suzhou, went to pay respects at the Weng house, and called Weng “maternal grandfather.” Weng paid him no attention. He asked to have his stepmother come out to see him; she also refused to come out. Fellow merchants were all angry and egged him on: “Your father paid eight hundred taels as betrothal, were husband and wife only four years, and before mourning was complete she was remarried to someone else. What harm is there in coming out once to see you? The feeling is hateful! Why not report it to the officials?” Qin then accused him before Street-Patrolling Censor Cai. By then Weng Bin’er, having gained Shi as a son-in-law, had revived the family style and put out over a thousand more in capital; seeing the accusation, he had not the slightest fear. Both sides used connections and sued for nearly two years. All the circuit and provincial offices took bribes and judged by stretching the facts. Later Qin filed with the Ministry of Justice, and only then got a fair judgment: “Weng Bin’er offset eight hundred taels with his daughter—almost the same price as Lüzhu, the famously costly concubine. But Shouxun consented of his own will; we will not discuss the betrothal wealth. Now, before the husband’s mourning was complete, she was remarried to merchant Liang, scooping up more goods—this is treating a daughter as merchandise, with no regard for the law. He should be beaten thirty strokes; we award body-price silver of one hundred taels, plus the fifty taels Shouxun spent on clothes and ornaments for Yunying, all to be received by Shi Qin.” Because of years of piled-up lawsuits, Bin’er’s family wealth was entirely gone, and he fell back into poverty.

paragraphs.zh: 按：脱骗之害，首侠棍，次狡侩。侠棍设局暗脱，窃盗也。狡侩骗货明卖，强盗也。二者当与盗同科。凡牙侩之弊，客货入店，彼皆作纲抵偿，又多窃取供家，每以后客货盖前客帐，此穷牙常态也。施守训在不早审牙家，致落此坑堑。只可小心逼取，或继以告，不当图其女为妾。夫以六旬上人，岁月几何，纳妾异地，能无后患乎？贻子后讼，所费不资。虽最终取胜，得不偿失矣。独恨翁滨二负心歹汉，以一女而还银八百两，得已过分，又得婿扶以成家；后女虽再嫁，当以身资还施之男，永可无患矣。乃贪心不满，再致倾家，真可为欺心负义之鉴。
paragraphs.en: Note: Among the harms of stripping and swindling, first come swaggering ruffians, then cunning brokers. Swaggering ruffians set traps and strip in the dark—that is theft. Cunning brokers cheat you of goods and sell them in the open—that is robbery. Both should be punished like bandits. As for the tricks of brokers: once a client’s goods enter the shop, they use them as a batch to offset debts, and also steal much for household use; they always cover earlier clients’ accounts with later clients’ goods. This is the usual way of a poor broker. Shi Shouxun’s fault was not checking the broker’s house early, so he fell into this pit. He should only have pressed carefully for payment, or followed with a lawsuit; he should not have schemed to take the daughter as concubine. A man past sixty—how many years does he have left? Taking a concubine in a strange place—can there be no later trouble? He left his son a later lawsuit, and the costs were enormous. Though he finally won, the gain did not cover the loss. What is hateful is Weng Bin’er, a heartless scoundrel: with one daughter he repaid eight hundred taels, already more than enough, and then got a son-in-law’s help to rebuild the household. Later, even if the girl remarried, he should have given the body-price back to Shi’s son, and there would have been no trouble forever. But his greedy heart was not satisfied, and he brought on the ruin of his house. Truly a mirror for those who cheat the heart and betray duty.

stories.title_en: A Poor Broker Dumps Wax to Pay Old Debts

paragraphs.zh: 张霸，四川人。为人机关精密，身长力勇。一日，买蜡百餘担，往福建建宁府丘店发卖。此牙家盆彻骨，外张富态，欠前客货银极多。霸蜡到，即以光棍顶作鬼名来借蜡，约后还银。数日后，霸往街游玩，其蜡遍在诸铺。及问其姓名，皆与帐名不同。霸心疑必有弊，故回店讯问牙人曰：“你脱我蜡去还前帐，可一一实报帐来。若不实言，你乘我几拳不得。”丘牙哑口无应。霸轮拳擒打，如鹰擒雀，如踢戏球。丘牙连忙求饶，曰：“公神人也。此蜡真还前客旧帐，并家用去矣，何能问各店重取？”张霸曰：“你将还人的及各店买去的，都登上帐，只说他揭借去，俱未还银。我将帐去告，取你硬作证，怕他各店不再还我？”丘牙依言，一一写成发货帐。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba was a man of Sichuan. His schemes were fine and close; he was tall and strong. One day he bought more than a hundred loads of wax and went to sell it at the Qiu shop in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. This broker’s house was poor to the bone, but outwardly put on a rich look, and owed a great deal of silver for earlier clients’ goods. When Ba’s wax arrived, they had ruffians come under dummy names to “borrow” the wax, promising to pay silver later. A few days later Ba walked the streets for amusement, and his wax was in shops all over. When he asked their names, none matched the names on the account. Ba suspected there must be a trick, so he went back to the shop and questioned the broker: “You dumped my wax to pay old accounts. Report the accounts one by one, truthfully. If you do not tell the truth, you will not get away with a few of my punches.” Broker Qiu was dumbstruck. Ba swung his fists and beat him, like a hawk seizing a sparrow, like kicking a play-ball. Qiu hurriedly begged for mercy: “You are a spirit, sir. This wax truly went to pay earlier clients’ old accounts, and for household use besides. How can I go to the shops and take it back?” Zhang Ba said: “Put down on the account what you repaid people and what the shops bought; just say they took it on credit and have not yet paid the silver. I will take the account and file a complaint, and have you firmly testify. Are you afraid those shops will not pay me again?” Qiu followed his words and wrote out the dispatch-of-goods account one by one.

paragraphs.zh: 张霸即具状告府。署印梅爷看状，掷地不准。霸心伤失本，两眼自然垂。再三哀告，梅爷乃准其状。先差皂隶往查各店蜡。霸以银贿公差，回报曰：“各店果有张霸印号蜡。”梅爷曰：“哪有揭借客蜡都不还银者！”即出牌拘审。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba then filed a complaint at the prefecture. Acting prefect Master Mei looked at the complaint, threw it on the ground, and would not accept it. Ba was wounded at heart over losing his capital; tears fell of themselves. After he pleaded again and again, Master Mei accepted the complaint. He first sent yamen runners to check the wax in the shops. Ba bribed the runners with silver; they reported back: “The shops do indeed have wax with Zhang Ba’s stamp.” Master Mei said: “How can there be people who take a client’s wax on credit and never pay the silver!” He issued a warrant to arrest and try them.

paragraphs.zh: 各店在外商量曰：“我店买张客蜡，俱已还银，牙家收讫。又牙人自用蜡还我者，是他所合抽得牙钱，何得今更重告？吾与汝等敛银共用，投一分上，先去讲明，然后对审。”敛银已毕，即将银一百两投梅爷乡亲。
paragraphs.en: The shops conferred outside: “Our shops bought merchant Zhang’s wax and have already paid the silver; the broker received it. And the wax the broker himself used to repay us was what he had as his brokerage cut. How can he now sue us again? Let us pool silver to use together, send a connection in first to explain, then confront them at trial.” When the silver was collected, they sent one hundred taels to a fellow-townsman of Master Mei.

paragraphs.zh: 梅爷刚正之官，弗听，即拘来审。内有江店客人，乃惯讼者，先对理曰：“蜡乃丘牙明卖与我，公平交易，张霸安得重取？即未全交付，亦牙家刻落，与我辈何干？”丘牙曰：“蜡非卖他。是小人先欠诸店旧帐，张霸蜡到，他等诈言措借，数日后即还银。及得蜡到手，即坐以抵前帐。非小人敢兜客银也。”梅爷曰：“丘牙欠债，须问彼自取，安得坐客人货以还彼债？你众等可将价还张霸，免你等罪。”江店恃有分上，再三辩论，说是明白交易，并无对债之事。梅爷触怒，将江店责十板；江店又辩论不已，又被责二十板。后诸人惊惧，皆称愿赔求饶。以江店监禁，诸人讨保，断蜡银，限三日，不完再重责。三日果追完。霸领银讫，深感梅爷恩泽，顶戴香炉，到于堂下，叩拜而去。
paragraphs.en: Master Mei was an upright official and would not listen. He had them brought for trial. Among them was a client of the Jiang shop, used to lawsuits, who first argued: “The wax was openly sold to me by broker Qiu, a fair deal. How can Zhang Ba take it a second time? Even if it was not fully handed over, that is the broker’s skimming—what has it to do with us?” Broker Qiu said: “The wax was not sold to them. This humble person first owed the shops old accounts. When Zhang Ba’s wax arrived, they falsely said they would borrow it and pay silver in a few days. Once they had the wax in hand, they sat on it to offset the old accounts. It is not that this humble person dared pocket the client’s silver.” Master Mei said: “If broker Qiu owes debts, they should collect from him. How can they sit on a client’s goods to repay his debts? You lot will pay the price to Zhang Ba, and I will spare you punishment.” The Jiang shop, relying on the connection, argued again and again that it was a clear sale, with no offsetting of debts. Master Mei was angered, beat the Jiang shop ten strokes; Jiang still would not stop arguing, and was beaten another twenty. Then the others were frightened and all said they were willing to pay and begged for mercy. Jiang was jailed; the others found guarantors. The wax silver was judged due in three days; if not complete, they would be heavily beaten again. In three days it was indeed collected in full. Ba received the silver, deeply grateful for Master Mei’s kindness; he wore an incense brazier on his head, went before the hall, kowtowed, and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：出外为商，以缥缈之身，涉寡亲之境，全仗经纪以为耳目。若遇经纪公正，则货物有主；一投狡侩，而抑货亏价必矣。是择经纪，乃经商一大关系也，可不慎哉！如其人言谈直率，此是公正之人。若初会晤间，上下估看，方露微言，则其心中狡猾可知。若价即言而不远，应对迟慢，心必怀欺。若屋宇精致，分外巧样，多是奢华务外之人，内必不能积聚。倘衣补垢腻，人鄙形猥，肩耸目光，巾帽不称寒暑，此皆贫穷之辈。若巧异妆扮，服色变常，必非创置之人，其内必无财钞。若衣冠不华，惟服布衣，此乃老实本分，不可以斯之曰贫。商而知此，何至如张霸，被牙所脱也？况非刚正之梅爷，肯听分上，几乎素手归矣。故录之，以示为商者。当货物发脱之初，细审经纪对手，发落方可保无虞矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: When you go out as a merchant, a body adrift in a place with few kin, you rely entirely on the broker as your eyes and ears. If you meet an honest broker, the goods have a master; once you fall in with a cunning broker, the goods will be held down and the price shorted, that is certain. So choosing a broker is a great matter in trade—can you not be careful? If a man’s talk is straight and frank, he is an honest man. If at the first meeting he looks you up and down, and only then lets out a few words, you can tell his mind is sly. If he names a price at once and it is not far off, but answers slowly, his heart must hold deceit. If the house is finely built, extra-clever in style, he is likely a man of luxury who tends to outward show, and inwardly cannot accumulate. If his clothes are patched and greasy, his person mean and his form ugly, shoulders hunched and eyes staring, cap and kerchief not matching the season—these are all the poor. If he dresses in odd, clever ways, colors and clothes out of the ordinary, he is surely not a man who has built anything up, and inwardly he has no cash. If his cap and gown are not showy, and he wears only cloth, this is an honest, proper man; you cannot call him poor on that account. If a merchant knows this, how would he come to be like Zhang Ba, stripped by a broker? Besides, if it had not been the upright Master Mei, who refused to hear connections, he would nearly have gone home empty-handed. So I record this to show merchants: at the very start when goods are to be sold off, look closely at the broker you deal with; only then can you dispatch the goods without worry.

stories.title_en: Alarming Words Goad a Man Back to Gambling

paragraphs.zh: 张士升，莒溪人，膏粱子弟也。父致万金，均分于士升兄弟，田园膏腴，坐享成业。一旦父卒，时初行万历钱，被棍徒引其赌博。彼富豪雏子，惟见场中饮酒豪放，可轻狂快意，哪知财帛当惜？不数月间，输去银数百两，尚欣欣喜赌，未肯休也。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Shisheng, of Juxi, was a son of rich food and fine clothes. His father had made ten thousand taels, divided equally among Shisheng and his brothers; the fields and gardens were rich, and they sat enjoying a finished estate. Once the father died, just when Wanli cash was first in use, ruffians lured him into gambling. That greenhorn son of a rich house saw only the drinking and swagger in the gambling den, which felt light, wild, and pleasing—how would he know money should be treasured? Within a few months he had lost several hundred taels of silver, and still went to gamble with a glad heart, unwilling to stop.

paragraphs.zh: 乡有陈荣一者，乃士升父在日所用做中保供呼唤者。人虽微贱，却有忠义之心，不忍士升之被棍诱引也。乃备一盛筵，单请士升一人，酒筵中慢慢缓谈，将其父在日，始终生财缘由，爱惜钱米实事，一一从头细讲；且赞羡其能，慨叹其苦，后又谈及民情世故，及钱米难得之状，穷民无钱之苦，因劝之曰：“令先尊发此巨富非易，你须念先人勤劳，保守基业，切不可去赌。前者虽赌去数百金，已往勿咎；但从今改过，依旧坐享福泽矣。”士升见荣一词情恳切，一时良心发动，曰：“吾依你言，从今誓不赌也。”次日棍徒引之，果不去赌。众方怪异，后知出于荣一所劝，无可奈何，商议曰：“谁能引其再赌者，众敛十金与之。”有柴昆者曰：“我能引之。”众将银十两封存。
paragraphs.en: In the village was Chen Rongyi, whom Shisheng’s father in his lifetime had used as a middleman and errand-runner. Though of low station, he had a loyal heart and could not bear to see Shisheng lured by ruffians. He prepared a rich banquet and invited Shisheng alone. Over the wine he slowly talked, telling from the beginning how the father had made his money, and the real facts of how he treasured cash and rice, going through it one by one; he praised his ability, sighed over his hardships, then spoke of popular feeling and worldly affairs, how hard cash and rice are to come by, the suffering of the poor who have no money, and so advised him: “It was not easy for your late honored father to make this great wealth. You must think of the ancestors’ toil and keep the foundation. You must not go gamble. Though you gambled away several hundred taels before, let the past not be blamed; from today, if you change, you can still sit and enjoy good fortune.” Shisheng saw Rongyi’s words were earnest; for a moment conscience stirred, and he said: “I will follow your words. From today I swear I will not gamble.” The next day the ruffians came to lead him; indeed he would not go. They were all astonished; later they learned it was Rongyi’s advice, and could do nothing. They conferred: “Whoever can lead him to gamble again, we will pool ten taels for him.” A man named Chai Kun said: “I can lead him.” They sealed up ten taels of silver to keep.

paragraphs.zh: 昆见士升在路亭闲坐，挨近其身，先闲谈他事，后问曰：“闻汝今收手不赌乎？”士升曰：“然。”昆曰：“赌非好事，今能自知回头，真是豪杰。盛族富家子弟，果有知识高人，我真羡服！只外人都传，是荣一老劝你而止。果是他劝否？”士升曰：“的是得他劝。”柴昆嗟叹曰：“荣一小辈奔走下贱之流，岂是你父兄，岂是你叔伯，何禁止得人？你名门子弟，聪明男子，何待贱人训诲？使路人传你听下贱人主使，皆暗中非笑，谓你无能为。依我所见，还当暂出小赌，过了半月一月，自己收手，人便说你是自不爱赌，非关听下辈命令也。如此方是大丈夫所为，不羞了故家门风。”士升是无识雏子，闻此佞言，心自猜曰：“果是我今若便止，人道是荣一之功。须再去赌一月，然后自止，岂不挺豪杰哉！”随即入场复赌。柴昆暗领众银而去。
paragraphs.en: Kun saw Shisheng sitting idle in a roadside pavilion, drew near him, first chatted of other things, then asked: “I hear you have now folded your hand and do not gamble?” Shisheng said: “That is so.” Kun said: “Gambling is no good thing. Now that you know to turn back yourself, you are truly a hero. A son of a great clan and rich house, with knowledge above others—I truly admire you! Only outsiders all say it was old Rongyi who advised you to stop. Was it really his advice?” Shisheng said: “It truly was his advice.” Chai Kun sighed: “Rongyi is a petty runner of the low sort. Is he your father or elder brother? Is he your uncle? How can he forbid a man? You are a son of a famous house, a clever fellow—why wait for a low man’s instruction? If people on the road say you take orders from a low man, they all laugh at you behind your back, saying you have no ability. In my view, you should still go out for a little gambling. After half a month or a month, stop of your own accord, and people will say you yourself do not love gambling, not that you obeyed a lesser man’s command. That is what a true man does, and it will not shame the old family style.” Shisheng was a greenhorn without knowledge. Hearing this flattery, he guessed to himself: “Indeed, if I stop right now, people will say it was Rongyi’s merit. I should go gamble another month, then stop myself—would that not make me a real hero?” He went straight into the den and gambled again. Chai Kun secretly took the crowd’s silver and left.

paragraphs.zh: 士升赌了一月，野心复逞。后荣一虽言，亦不见纳，终至于尽赌倾家。皆柴昆一激之也，其祸烈也。
paragraphs.en: Shisheng gambled a month, and his wild heart broke out again. Later, though Rongyi spoke, he would not take it in, and in the end gambled until the house was emptied. All this was Chai Kun’s one goad; the disaster was fierce.

paragraphs.zh: 按：士升惑柴昆之瞽说，拒荣一之忠言，徒以其人卑微，谓受其谏为耻。不知尧请问下民，舜下询荛，周公走迎乎下士，韩信乞策于左车。彼帝王将相，犹俯听微言若是，岂以人之贱而可废其言之善乎！惜士升黄口之子，目不知古今，故中谗言而不察也。噫！
paragraphs.en: Note: Shisheng was confused by Chai Kun’s blind talk and rejected Rongyi’s loyal words, merely because the man was lowly, and thought it shameful to take his counsel. He did not know that Yao inquired of the common people, Shun asked down to the grass-cutters, the Duke of Zhou hurried out to meet lesser gentlemen, and Han Xin begged plans from Li Zuoche. Those emperors, kings, and generals still bent to hear humble words like that—can you discard a good word because the man is low? Pity that Shisheng was a yellow-mouthed boy who knew nothing of past and present, so he fell for slander and did not see it. Alas!

stories.title_en: Posing as a Young Lord, Using a Courtesan to Strip a Gambler

paragraphs.zh: 王荻溪，万金之子。好赌无厌，多被赌朋合谋，尽倾其家。后收拾餘资，只得三百两，乃带一仆，复往县中赌。众棍后合本，迭来与赌。时荻溪家已尽破，而赌已学得甚高，虽未能胜众棍，亦不至为棍所胜。相持半月余，无好子弟到，无雏家可网，乃投府去。更无大赌场可快意者，遂往嫖李细卿家。
paragraphs.en: Wang Dixi was the son of a ten-thousand-tael house. He loved gambling without satiety, and was often plotted against by gambling companions until his household was entirely emptied. Later he gathered the remaining capital, only three hundred taels, took one servant, and went back to the county town to gamble. The ruffians later pooled capital and came in turns to gamble with him. By then Dixi’s house was already broken, but he had learned to gamble very well; though he could not beat the pack of ruffians, he also would not be beaten by them. They held each other off more than half a month. With no good young gentlemen arriving, no greenhorns to net, they went off to the prefectural city. There was still no large gambling den to satisfy him, so he went to visit the courtesan Li Xiqing’s house.

paragraphs.zh: 有二三赌伙寻至府，闻荻溪已入妓家，众即划计曰：“如此如此笼络之，可尽夺其金矣。”次日，候荻溪出外寻赌伙，即入对细卿曰：“荻溪只好赌，不好嫖，彼无厚物与你。今依我如此如此行，先送你二十两人事。后赌得的，每一百两复许加二抽。”细卿许诺，午设盛馔，方与荻溪入席饮数杯。忽二家人来送礼物，辉煌熳烂，皆上好物件，约值二十餘金。曰：“公子命送此薄仪，少倾便到。”细卿逐一看过，尽数收起，以茶待二家人于外，复来席陪荻溪，且喜且作懊恼之意。荻溪曰：“是何人送你厚礼，你反似犹闷，何故？”细卿曰：“不问正难开口。此是黄公子送的。旧年在此赌钱，输去银千餘两，我亦得他厚惠。今日将到，望相公赦我，妾须出去迎他。容后日多陪相公几日，以补罪。”荻溪曰：“既是公子，我便出外让他。”细卿喜曰：“相公如此宽容，是妾有二天也。”荻溪将拂衣起，细卿挽住曰：“少坐不妨！更有一件，此人极活泼无崖岸。少间乘机提起，若请相见，或在此同话，为我陪客。得借重高贤，亦为我增声价也。”荻溪本欲避席，只闻公子旧在此赌，心中早已喜十分。使一仆伏侍，在内独酌，叫细卿出外迎客。
paragraphs.en: Two or three gambling partners tracked him to the prefecture. Hearing Dixi had entered a courtesan’s house, they laid a plan: “If we snare him thus and so, we can take all his gold.” The next day they waited until Dixi went out looking for gambling partners, then went in and said to Xiqing: “Dixi only likes gambling, not whoring; he has no rich gifts for you. Now do as we say, thus and so. First we send you twenty taels as a present. Later, of whatever is won at gambling, for every hundred taels we promise you another twenty percent cut.” Xiqing agreed. At noon she set a rich meal; just as she and Dixi had drunk a few cups, suddenly two household servants came with gifts, glittering and splendid, all first-rate things, worth over twenty taels. They said: “The young lord ordered us to send this small token; he will be here shortly.” Xiqing looked them over one by one, put them all away, served tea to the two servants outside, then came back to the table to keep Dixi company, looking both pleased and as if vexed. Dixi said: “Who sent you such rich gifts, that you instead look gloomy? Why?” Xiqing said: “If you had not asked, it would be hard to open my mouth. These are from Young Lord Huang. Last year he gambled here and lost over a thousand taels; I also received his rich favors. He is about to arrive today. I hope you will pardon me, sir; I must go out to receive him. Allow me in days to come to keep you company extra days, to make up the offense.” Dixi said: “Since it is a young lord, I will go outside and yield to him.” Xiqing happily said: “If you are so forbearing, sir, I have a second heaven.” Dixi was about to rise and shake out his sleeves; Xiqing held him back: “Sit a little; it does not matter! There is one more thing. This man is extremely lively, with no airs. In a moment, if the chance comes up and he asks to meet you, or talks here together, keep the guest company for me. If I may borrow your worthy presence, it will also raise my standing.” Dixi had meant to leave the table, but hearing the young lord had gambled here before, his heart was already ten parts pleased. He had one servant wait on him, drank alone inside, and told Xiqing to go out and receive the guest.

paragraphs.zh: 须臾，公子到，细卿从容奉茶。叙寒温讫，公子径起，欲入内游玩。细卿慌忙请止，曰：“适有一外亲远来，在内留一水饭，恐无处可避也。”公子笑曰：“孤老便是孤老，何须托外亲也？既是你情人，我生平不吃醋，便请相见何妨？”即遣二仆入请。尚未出，又促细卿曰：“汝去请之。”细卿入内邀出。公子张看荻溪一表非俗，呵呵笑曰：“细卿妙人，果会择好才子。”即降前叙礼，院内备筵已到，公子坐上，荻溪前，细卿左陪。席间谈笑，并不及赌中去。到晚，索骰子行令，公子耍曰：“只恐卑人未晓好色。”细卿曰：“公子有一掷百万之豪，荻卿亦有呼庐赐绯之兴，愧小婢未足当好色耳。”公子曰：“荻溪亦作家乎？明早略赌一东道何如？”荻溪曰：“东道当小弟奉，何劳赌也？”公子曰：“空食未佳，须赢为奇。”先取掷之，无色。荻溪一掷即胜。公子须再加一台戏，又输；热性一起，曰：“荻溪有此妙手乎！与汝再决输赢。”荻溪曰：“不敢扳高耳，亦愿陪。”两下赌起，互有胜负。
paragraphs.en: In a moment the young lord arrived. Xiqing calmly served tea. After the greetings of heat and cold, the young lord rose at once, wanting to go inside to stroll. Xiqing hurriedly asked him to stop: “Just now a kinsman from elsewhere has come from far away; he is inside having a simple meal. I fear there is nowhere to hide him.” The young lord laughed: “A kept man is a kept man; why pretend he is an outside kinsman? Since he is your lover, I am not jealous in my life—what harm in asking him to meet?” He sent two servants in to invite. They had not yet come out; he again urged Xiqing: “You go invite him.” Xiqing went in and invited him out. The young lord looked Wang Dixi over—a distinguished appearance, not common—and laughed: “Xiqing is a clever one; she does know how to pick a fine talent.” He came forward, exchanged courtesies. A banquet was already prepared in the courtyard. The young lord sat at the head, Dixi in front, Xiqing accompanying on the left. Through the meal they talked and laughed, never touching on gambling. At evening they called for dice to play drinking games. The young lord joked: “I only fear a humble man like me does not yet know good sport.” Xiqing said: “The young lord has the spirit to throw a million at a toss; Dixi also has the zest of calling the dice and granting scarlet. I, a little maid, am ashamed I am not equal to ‘good sport.’” The young lord said: “Is Dixi also a practiced hand? Tomorrow morning, shall we gamble a little treat?” Dixi said: “The treat should be this younger brother’s to offer; why bother gambling?” The young lord said: “Eating for nothing is no good; winning is what is remarkable.” He took the dice and threw first—no points. Dixi won in one throw. The young lord had to add another stage of opera, and lost again. Heat rose in him: “Dixi has such a fine hand! Let us decide win and loss once more.” Dixi said: “I dare not climb high, but I am willing to keep you company.” The two began to gamble, each winning and losing in turn.

paragraphs.zh: 至一更，公子输上百金。细卿亦抽头十餘两矣，即将骰子收起，曰：“今日乘轿劳顿，夜已深矣，须去睡。明日看戏时酒席中再翻，稍抬举我抽头。”公子以输多，发怒要赌。荻溪亦发大言曰：“若再来，须百金一堆，不然且罢！”公子先取定银在，以一百为堆。细卿故执骰不与。公子大怒曰：“只凭一掷，随有无便罢！”细卿付还骰。公子一掷即胜，得百金，曰：“更照前一堆。”又胜；曰：“我生平好大不好细，须二百为堆。”方发性间，忽闻门外火把轿来。慌入报曰：“老爷跟寻至急，可速回去！”公子曰：“我色方来，奈何阻我兴！”其后一掷，又赢二百为堆。家人催如星火，公子曰：“我明日昼间不来，夜定来矣。”荻溪留之，不能得。细卿亦惊作痴呆样，慌忙送别。归怨荻溪曰：“人无全胜。你先赢许多，须当知止。奈何公子欲翻，你更出大堆，是不晓避色也。空作惯家，不及我妇人见矣。”荻溪曰：“吾万金赌尽，何数他三百两！有甚大事，空怨恨为！”在细卿家留宿数日；再留之，坚辞而去。
paragraphs.en: By the first watch the young lord had lost over a hundred taels. Xiqing had also taken a cut of more than ten taels. She then gathered up the dice and said: “Today you were tired from riding in a sedan; the night is already deep; you should go sleep. Tomorrow when we watch the play, we can reverse it over the banquet, and you can raise me a little in the cut.” The young lord, having lost much, grew angry and insisted on gambling. Dixi also made a big speech: “If we go on, it must be a hundred taels a pile; otherwise let it be!” The young lord already had fixed silver on him, and made a hundred a pile. Xiqing deliberately held the dice and would not give them. The young lord raged: “Just one throw, and whether there is anything or not, we stop!” Xiqing handed the dice back. The young lord won in one throw, got a hundred taels, said: “Another pile as before.” He won again; said: “All my life I like the large, not the small; it must be two hundred a pile.” Just as the heat was rising, suddenly they heard torches and a sedan at the gate. Someone rushed in to report: “His Lordship is searching most urgently; you must go back at once!” The young lord said: “My luck has just come—why stop my sport!” His next throw won another two-hundred pile. The servants urged like shooting stars. The young lord said: “I will not come in the daytime tomorrow; at night I will surely come.” Dixi tried to keep him, but could not. Xiqing also pretended to be stunned with fright, hurriedly saw him off, then came back and blamed Dixi: “No one wins all the time. You first won a great deal; you should have known to stop. Why, when the young lord wanted to reverse it, did you put out even bigger piles? That is not knowing how to dodge luck. You call yourself a practiced hand, but you do not even match this woman’s insight.” Dixi said: “I gambled away ten thousand taels; what are his three hundred to me! What great matter is it, that you should empty your resentment?” He stayed several nights at Xiqing’s house; when she asked him to stay longer, he firmly declined and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：公子是装来的，先以厚礼送妓，令荻溪信为真公子。后来圈套，皆是装成。其药骰已先藏在细卿手，故令其抢起真骰，然后以药骰付还之，使其不疑。三执皆胜，套定催归，其谁防之？然荻溪虽作家，安能测其弊哉！吁！凡赌博者，弊外生弊，鉴此而知机，收手勿赌，真良策也，莫如彼之一旦尽囊而空矣！
paragraphs.en: Note: The young lord was a put-up job. First they sent rich gifts to the courtesan, to make Dixi believe he was a real young lord. The later trap was all staged. Loaded dice had already been hidden in Xiqing’s hand, so she was made to snatch up the true dice, then hand back the loaded ones, so he would not suspect. Three throws, all wins; then they set it that he was urged home—who would guard against that? Yet even though Dixi was a practiced hand, how could he fathom the cheat? Alas! For all gamblers, cheat breeds cheat outside of cheat. Take warning from this, see the mechanism, fold your hand and do not gamble—that is the true good plan. Do not be like him, emptied of his purse in a single day!

stories.title_en: A Lover of Gambling Falls into Someone Else’s Trick

paragraphs.zh: 闽人徐华胜，号含秀。为人矜夸骄亢，酷好赌钱。一日，买纸往京卖。有张鄂号叔真者，先富，因赌倾折，后有餘囊数百两，亦买纸往京卖。二人同县异乡，托处共店。鄂心怀一术，每在店中与华胜着棋，或赌东道，或赌时果。鄂棋本能让华胜一车，鄂乃孤客，徐姓众多，鄂每诈输东道，暗结华之乡亲，使钳其口，无得而议论之。故输五而赢二，而华胜不知鄂怀锋而之。
paragraphs.en: Xu Huasheng of Min, style Hanxiu, was boastful and arrogant, and fiercely loved gambling. One day he bought paper to sell in the capital. There was Zhang E, style Shuzhen, once rich, broken by gambling, later with a remaining purse of several hundred taels, who also bought paper to sell in the capital. The two were of the same county but different townships, and lodged in the same shop. E had a scheme in mind. He often played chess with Huasheng in the shop, sometimes betting a treat, sometimes betting seasonal fruit. E’s chess could actually give Huasheng a one-chariot handicap, but E was a lone traveler, while the Xu surname were many. E often pretended to lose the treat, secretly befriended Xu’s fellow-townsmen so they would clamp their mouths and not discuss it. So he lost five and won two, and Huasheng did not know E came carrying a hidden edge.

paragraphs.zh: 一日，鄂已睡，华胜邀起而赌东道。鄂心喜曰：“此夜机会可矣。”故推不起。又强之，鄂曰：“我不赌东道，要赌银。”胜心暗忖：“我棋高他，何惧之有？”连声应曰：“更好。”不知已堕其术矣。且素性亢傲，乡亲咸憎之，大家赞成其赌。鄂曰：“先以银对定，输即收去，无得抵赖。要一两一局，每两与众抽头二钱，作东道并做戏。”胜曰：“虽二两无妨。”未几，输数局。心中热起，说要十两一局。客中老成者曰：“不可，且休矣！”其后生辈反以言激之。胜心益热，再对银十两而赌。不数局，共输数十餘两。时天色已曙，鄂将胜银卷入囊中而起。胜邀再赌，鄂坚执不许，二人相扭甚热。鄂曰：“是你邀我赌，非我邀你赌。我若输你，肯饶否？我家财数千，因赌而倾。你输此些小，何得鼻血？好不为男子也！任你经官不还。”客中老成者曰：“是我辈无见识，不阻你，以致覆败。但张兄说得是，倘他输你，必不放他。不如我辈抽头者尽还你罢。俗云‘豪杰对豪杰，齿打落，吞肚里’。”鄂曰：“众既以抽头者退出，我亦退银三两做戏，更出一两作东道。内抽五钱，换金一线，打一戒指与徐兄，作好赌之戒。”众曰：“张兄之言大有理，乃豪杰惜豪杰，真慷慨丈夫也！”华胜默然。真个是：“安分不贪难诱引，贪心萌内必遭殃。”
paragraphs.en: One day E had already gone to sleep; Huasheng invited him up to gamble a treat. E was glad at heart: “Tonight the chance is here.” So he declined to get up. They pressed him again. E said: “I will not gamble for a treat; I want to gamble silver.” Sheng thought secretly: “My chess is better than his; what is there to fear?” He answered at once: “Even better.” He did not know he had already fallen into the trap. Besides, by nature he was arrogant; his fellow-townsmen all disliked him, and they all cheered the gamble. E said: “First match silver against silver; whoever loses, it is taken at once, no welching. One tael a game; of each tael, two mace go to the company as a cut, for a treat and for putting on a play.” Sheng said: “Even two taels would be no harm.” Before long he lost several games. Heat rose in him, and he said he wanted ten taels a game. The older, steadier guests said: “You must not; stop for now!” The younger set instead goaded him with words. Sheng’s heart grew hotter; he matched another ten taels and gambled. In a few games he had lost several tens of taels in all. By then the sky was already light. E rolled Sheng’s silver into his bag and got up. Sheng invited him to gamble more; E firmly refused. The two tussled, quite heated. E said: “You invited me to gamble, not I you. If I had lost to you, would you have let me off? My family wealth was several thousand, and gambling emptied it. You lost this little bit—why the nosebleed? A fine man you are not! Go to the officials if you like; I will not pay it back.” The older guests said: “It was we who had no sense, and did not stop you, so you came to this defeat. But Brother Zhang is right: if he had lost to you, he surely would not have let you go. Better that we who took the cut give it all back to you. As the saying goes, ‘Hero to hero: if teeth are knocked out, swallow them.’” E said: “Since the company is giving back the cut, I will also give back three taels for a play, and put out one tael more for a treat. From that, take five mace, change it for a thread of gold, and make a ring for Brother Xu, as a warning against loving to gamble.” All said: “Brother Zhang’s words are most reasonable—hero cherishing hero, a truly generous man!” Huasheng was silent. Truly it is: “If you keep your lot and do not greed, you are hard to lure; once greed sprouts within, you will surely meet disaster.”

paragraphs.zh: 按：好赌者落人圈套，何止若是。鄂犹是有本富商，故不尽取，而又善处于终，致戒其后。若赌场中光棍，何怕你万贯家财，尽落于伊手乎！睹徐华胜之输而返悔者，后人鉴之，可勿蹈矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Those who love gambling fall into others’ traps—and not only like this. E was still a merchant who had once had capital, so he did not take everything, and also handled the ending well, leaving a warning for afterward. If it had been a gambling-den ruffian, what would he care if you had ten thousand strings of cash? It would all fall into his hands! Look at Xu Huasheng, who lost and then regretted: later people should take warning, and not follow the same path.

stories.title_en: Posing as a Young Lord to Steal a Merchant’s Silver

paragraphs.zh: 陈栋，山东人也，屡年入福建建阳地名长埂贩买机布。万历三十二年季春，同二仆带银壹千馀两，复往长埂买布。途逢一棍，窥其银多，欲谋之。见栋乃老练惯客，每迟行早宿，关防严密，难以动手。诈称福建分巡建南道公子，甚有规模态度，乃带四仆，一路与栋同店。棍不与栋交语，而栋亦不之顾也。
paragraphs.en: Chen Dong was a man of Shandong. For years he went to Changgeng in Jianyang, Fujian, to buy loom cloth. In the third month of Wanli 32, with two servants and over a thousand taels of silver, he again went to Changgeng to buy cloth. On the way he met a ruffian who spied that he had much silver and wanted to scheme for it. Seeing Dong was a seasoned old traveler, always starting late and lodging early, with tight precautions, it was hard to make a move. He pretended to be the son of the Fujian Circuit Intendant of Jiannan Circuit, with quite the air and manner, and brought four servants, lodging at the same inns as Dong all the way. The ruffian did not speak with Dong, and Dong paid him no attention.

paragraphs.zh: 直至江西铅山县，其县丞姓蔡名渊者，乃广东人也，与巡道同府异县，素不相识。棍往拜之。县丞闻是巡道公子，待之甚厚，即来回拜，送下程。栋见县丞回拜，信其为真公子。是夜，棍以下程请栋。栋欢领之，而心中犹谨防他盗，不敢痛饮；棍犹动手不得。次日，经乌石宿。其地非大口岸，栋欲办酒回礼，以无物可买而止。
paragraphs.en: Not until Yanshan county in Jiangxi: the assistant magistrate, Cai Yuan, was of Guangdong, of the same prefecture as the circuit intendant but a different county, and they had never met. The ruffian went to pay a call. The assistant magistrate, hearing it was the circuit intendant’s son, treated him very well, then came to return the call and sent traveling provisions. Dong saw the assistant magistrate return the call, and believed he was a true young lord. That night the ruffian invited Dong with the provisions. Dong gladly accepted, but in his heart still carefully guarded against thieves, and dared not drink hard; the ruffian still could not make a move. The next day they lodged at Wushi. It was not a large port; Dong wanted to prepare wine as a return courtesy, but had nothing to buy, so he stopped.

paragraphs.zh: 又次日，到崇安县宿。栋心谓：此到长埂旧主不远，犹其外之故家也。且来日与公子别矣，不答敬殊非礼也，遂买肴馔请之。棍谓栋曰：“同舟过江，前缘非偶。与君一路同来，岂非偶乎？明日与君分路，燕鸿南北，未知何日再会，各开怀畅饮。”延至三更，其仆皆困顿熟睡。栋醉甚，亦伏桌睡。棍遂将栋之财物悉偷去。
paragraphs.en: The day after, they lodged at Chong’an county. Dong thought: from here to my old host at Changgeng is not far, like an old family outside. And tomorrow I part from the young lord; not to return the courtesy would be quite unmannerly. So he bought dishes and invited him. The ruffian said to Dong: “Crossing the river in the same boat, the former affinity was no accident. Coming all this way with you, sir—is that not affinity? Tomorrow we take separate roads, swallow south and goose north, who knows when we meet again. Let each open the heart and drink freely.” They stretched it to the third watch; the servants were all exhausted and sound asleep. Dong was very drunk and also slept slumped on the table. The ruffian then stole all of Dong’s goods.

paragraphs.zh: 待栋醒觉，不知棍何处去矣。即在崇安县告店家通同作弊。随即往江西广信府，告其县丞勾引光棍，而以原店家作证。县丞诉曰：“福建巡道实与我同府异县，其人姓氏，我素知之；但公子并未会面，他称其姓氏来拜我，我乃县丞小官，安得不回他拜，不送他赆？今至崇安已经数日，盗你银去，与我何干？”栋曰：“那棍一路同来，我防之甚切。他来谒你，而你回拜，我方信是真公子，故堕其术。今其人系你相识，安得不告你？”本府不能判断。栋又在史大巡处告。史爷判是县丞不合错拜公子，轻易便送下程，致误客商，不无公错。谅断银壹百两，与栋作盘缠之资而归。
paragraphs.en: When Dong woke, he did not know where the ruffian had gone. He immediately accused the innkeeper at Chong’an of colluding in the cheat. Then he went to Guangxin Prefecture in Jiangxi and accused the assistant magistrate of drawing in a ruffian, using the original innkeeper as witness. The assistant magistrate pleaded: “The Fujian circuit intendant is indeed of my prefecture but a different county; I have long known his surname. But I had never met the son. He came calling under that surname. I am a small official, an assistant magistrate—how could I not return his call, not send him a farewell gift? By the time you reached Chong’an several days had passed; he stole your silver—what has that to do with me?” Dong said: “That ruffian came the whole way with me; I guarded against him most closely. He called on you, and you returned the call; only then did I believe he was a true young lord, and so I fell for the trick. Now the man is someone you know—how can I not accuse you?” The prefecture could not judge it. Dong then accused him before Regional Inspector Shi. Master Shi judged that the assistant magistrate was wrong to have mistakenly paid respects to a “young lord” and lightly sent provisions, thus misleading a merchant; it was not without official fault. He reasonably awarded one hundred taels of silver for Dong as traveling money to go home.

paragraphs.zh: 噫：棍之设机巧矣！一路妆作公子，商人犹知防之。至拜县丞，而县丞回拜送赆，孰不以为真公子也？又先设机以请商人，则商人备礼以答敬，亦理所必然也。乃故缠饮，困其主仆，则乘夜行窃易矣。故曰其设机最巧也。使栋更能慎防一夜，则棍奸无所施。故慎始不如慎终，日乾更继以夕惕，斯可万无一失。不然，抱瓮汲井，几至井口而败其瓮，与不慎何异？吾愿为商者，处终如谨始可也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Ah—the ruffian’s trap was clever! All the way he dressed as a young lord, and the merchant still knew to guard against him. Once he called on the assistant magistrate, and the assistant magistrate returned the call and sent a gift, who would not take him for a true young lord? He also first laid a scheme to invite the merchant, so the merchant prepared a courtesy in return—that too was only natural. Then he deliberately stretched the drinking, tired out master and servants, and stealing by night became easy. So I say his trap was most clever. If Dong had been able to guard carefully one more night, the ruffian’s treachery would have had nowhere to work. So care at the start is not as good as care at the end; daytime diligence must be followed by evening caution, and then you may be safe in ten thousand. Otherwise, carrying a jar to draw from a well, you nearly reach the well-mouth and break the jar—how is that different from not being careful? I wish merchants, at the end, would be as careful as at the start.

stories.title_en: Showing Off Clothes and Dress Wakes a Thief’s Heart

paragraphs.zh: 游天生，徽州府人。丰采俊雅，好装饰。尝同一仆徐丁携本银五百馀两，往建宁府买铁。始到崇安县，搭一青流船，艄公名李雅，水手名翁迓。雅先以嫖赌破家，后无赖而撑船。其时船至建阳县，天生起岸，往拜乡亲。将衣箱打开，取出衣服鲜丽，所带用物俱美。雅一见生心。
paragraphs.en: You Tiansheng was a man of Huizhou Prefecture. He had a handsome, elegant air and loved to dress up. He once took one servant, Xu Ding, and more than five hundred taels of capital, going to Jianning Prefecture to buy iron. They first reached Chong’an county and hired a Qingliu boat; the boatman was named Li Ya, the sailor Weng Ya. Ya had first broken his household with whoring and gambling, then, with no resources, poled a boat. When the boat reached Jianyang county, Tiansheng went ashore to call on fellow-townsmen. He opened his clothes chest, took out bright, beautiful garments; everything he carried was fine. At one look Ya’s heart was stirred.

paragraphs.zh: 至晚，天生叫艄公买些酒馔。雅暗将陀陀花入酒中———陀陀花者，乃三年茄花也，人服此则昏迷不能语。是夜，天生主仆中了此毒，醉不能醒。三鼓时候，雅邀水手行谋。水手曰：“钱财有命，不可逆理妄求。倘若事泄，罪将安逃？吾不敢为也。”雅狠心一起，不听水手之阻，将其主仆推入深潭。天生淹死，徐丁幸饮酒少，入水复苏，颇识水性，水上岸。次日，搭后船往建宁府，即抱牌告于王大爷。当差捕兵六名，同徐丁到临江门去缉拿。临江门，乃建宁往来诸船凑集之口岸也。是时李雅谋财在手，正买酒上船，思量作乐。徐丁认得，即引捕兵擒锁，搜其赃物，尚在船中。遂并入赃，俱拿到府。
paragraphs.en: In the evening Tiansheng told the boatman to buy some wine and food. Ya secretly put tuotuo flowers in the wine—tuotuo flowers are the flowers of the three-year eggplant; if a person takes this, he falls into a stupor and cannot speak. That night master and servant Tiansheng were struck by this poison, drunk and unable to wake. At the third drum Ya invited the sailor to join the plot. The sailor said: “Money has its fate; you must not go against reason and seek it wildly. If the affair leaks, where will you flee the crime? I dare not do it.” A cruel heart rose in Ya; he would not hear the sailor’s blocking, and pushed master and servant into a deep pool. Tiansheng drowned. Xu Ding, luckily having drunk little, revived in the water; he knew something of swimming, and came up on the bank. The next day he took a later boat to Jianning Prefecture, and immediately presented a written complaint before Master Wang. Six constables were sent, going with Xu Ding to Linjiang Gate to arrest them. Linjiang Gate is the port where boats coming and going from Jianning gather. At that time Li Ya, with the plotted wealth in hand, was just buying wine to take aboard, thinking of making merry. Xu Ding recognized him, led the constables to seize and lock him, searched for the stolen goods—they were still on the boat. So they took him together with the loot to the prefecture.

paragraphs.zh: 王爷审问。雅见事露，难以推托，一概供招，攀及水手同谋。徐丁曰：“我当中毒时，酩酊不能言，如梦中，闻得水手劝阻，不与同谋，已先逃去。今若枉及此人，令后人不肯向善也。”王爷即将李雅责四十板收监，依律拟斩。其行李并原银，差防夫二名，同徐丁直解至天生家去。李雅次年冬季处决。后水手翁迓弃船归农，颇致丰足。雅以谋人而促死，迓以阻谏而全家，谚曰：“善有善报，恶有恶报”，信不虚也。
paragraphs.en: Master Wang interrogated. Ya saw the affair was out and hard to push off, confessed everything, and implicated the sailor as a co-plotter. Xu Ding said: “When I was poisoned, I was dead drunk and could not speak, as in a dream, but I heard the sailor advise against it, not joining the plot, and he had already fled first. If this man is now wrongly implicated, it will make later people unwilling to turn toward the good.” Master Wang then beat Li Ya forty strokes and jailed him, sentenced him to beheading according to the law. The luggage and original silver were sent with two escorts, together with Xu Ding, straight to Tiansheng’s home. Li Ya was executed in the winter of the following year. Later the sailor Weng Ya gave up the boat and returned to farming, and came to fair plenty. Ya, plotting against others, hastened his own death; Ya, by blocking and advising, preserved his whole household. The proverb says, “Good has a good reward, evil an evil reward”—truly it is not empty.

paragraphs.zh: 按：游天生之召祸，良由衣服华丽，致使贼艄垂涎。大凡孤客搭船，切须提防贼艄谋害。昼宜略睡，夜方易醒。煮菜暖酒，尤防放毒。服宜朴素，勿太炫耀。故老子曰：“良贾深藏若虚。”孔子曰：“以约失之者鲜。”此诚养德之言，抑亦远祸之道也。
paragraphs.en: Note: The disaster You Tiansheng brought on himself truly came from his gorgeous clothes, which made the thief-boatman drool. In general, a lone traveler taking a boat must carefully guard against a thief-boatman’s harm. By day one should sleep a little, so that by night one wakes easily. When they cook vegetables and warm wine, be especially wary of poison. Clothes should be plain; do not show off too much. So Laozi said: “A good merchant hides his goods as if he had nothing.” Confucius said: “Those who fail by being sparing are few.” These are truly words for cultivating virtue, and also a way to keep disaster far.
